body.observations: E0 default run r001 (weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1) shows udp_goodput_bps=300003200, udp_loss_frac=0.0, tcp_goodput_bps=668633114, drops_band1=92, tcp_retrans=92, link_util=1.0. UDP demand is 300 Mbps payload, which is well below the configured UDP share of 500 Mbps. TCP receives about 669 Mbps payload, much larger than the configured TCP share of 500 Mbps, so the scheduler appears to let TCP use UDP's idle share. The total payload plus packet overhead is close to 1 Gbps, so TCP is probably near the maximum possible once UDP is delivered without loss. The key unknowns are: (a) the minimum weightUdp that keeps UDP loss <=1%, (b) whether queuePkts can absorb UDP under-service, (c) whether TCP goodput is independent of weightUdp above that minimum, and (d) whether larger queues improve TCP goodput.

body.text: UDP loss threshold is near the UDP wire-rate demand (about 0.31 of the link). weightUdp=0.30 should cause UDP loss above 1%, while weightUdp=0.35 should keep UDP loss at or below 1%.
A large queue can absorb UDP under-service at weightUdp=0.30 and keep UDP loss <=1%, whereas a very small queue cannot.
At a UDP-safe weightUdp=0.35, increasing queuePkts from 100 to 1000 increases TCP goodput by reducing TCP queue drops.

decision_rules.rival: The scheduler strictly reserves weightUdp for UDP and does not give idle UDP share to TCP; at weightUdp=0.95 TCP would be limited to roughly 5% of the link.
The UDP loss threshold is much lower than 0.30, or the default queue fully absorbs the deficit at 0.30, so weightUdp=0.30 would also have UDP loss <=1%.

UDP loss is determined only by the average service deficit and queue size does not materially change the measured loss fraction; if the deficit is large, even queuePkts=1000 loses >1%, and if it is small, even queuePkts=4 loses <=1%.
Queue size does not materially affect TCP goodput at this scheduler setting, or a larger queue causes bufferbloat and does not improve throughput.

body.observations: The default run r001 has udp_goodput_bps=300003200, tcp_goodput_bps=668633114, udp_loss_frac=0.0, drops_band1=92, tcp_retrans=92, link_util=1.0. The r001 series shows UDP queue almost always empty (q_band0 0-1) while TCP queue is often near the 100-packet limit (q_band1 about 65-95, qmin_band1=65) and TCP drops accumulate about 9 per second. Weight sweep at queuePkts=100: w030 has UDP loss 2.0944% and TCP 674820128; w032/w033 have UDP loss 0 and TCP about 668633114; w035 has UDP loss 4e-06 and TCP 668634272; w095 has UDP loss 0 and TCP 668633114. Thus the scheduler appears to give TCP the unused UDP share, and UDP demand is near 0.32 of the scheduler service. Queue experiments: q4_w030 has UDP loss -4e-06 and zero UDP drops but TCP drops/retrans 3483 and TCP 668631955; q1000_w030 still has UDP loss 2.1228% with zero TCP drops and TCP 667027795; q1000_w035 has zero drops but TCP 660828979, lower than q100_w035. Therefore large queues do not improve TCP goodput here, and small queues can change UDP/TCP loss distribution in a non-obvious way.

body.explanation: The scheduler transfers unused UDP share to TCP when UDP is not backlogged, so TCP is not capped by 1-weightUdp at high UDP weights (C1, E1). Near the UDP demand threshold, however, UDP is backlogged and the scheduler gives UDP its configured share; the remaining share goes to TCP. Therefore, lowering weightUdp just below the UDP demand threshold lets UDP lose a small fraction of packets and frees that capacity for TCP, increasing TCP goodput. The tested UDP-loss boundary is between weightUdp=0.3030 and 0.3035: 0.3030 gives udp_loss_frac=0.011155 and tcp_goodput_bps=671928762, while 0.3035 gives udp_loss_frac=0.009736 and tcp_goodput_bps=671509421 (E3, C9). Thus weightUdp=0.3035 is the closest tested feasible point to the 1% UDP-loss boundary and gives the highest tested TCP goodput while satisfying udp_loss_frac <= 0.01. queuePkts=100 is adequate: larger queues did not improve TCP goodput at the threshold (E1, E3, C4), and very small queues either did not raise feasible TCP goodput or caused many TCP drops (E1, E2, E4). TcpCubic is safe because loss-based variants were tied at a UDP-safe scheduler setting, while BBR and Vegas underutilized the link (E2, C7).
body.holds_when: The fixed system parameters remain as in the brief: 1 Gbps link, 50 us one-way delay, 1500-byte MTU, fixed UDP application demand of 1400-byte packets at 300 Mbps, TCP always backlogged, scheduler behavior as observed, and measurement with seed=1 and duration=10. It also holds for nearby seeds tested at weightUdp=0.3030, where outputs changed only in the last few digits (E3).
body.breaks_when: It would change if UDP demand or packet size changes, if the scheduler strictly reserves UDP share instead of transferring idle share to TCP, if queue/scheduler service discipline changes, if the UDP-loss constraint is made stricter than 1%, or if different seeds/durations move the measured UDP-loss boundary enough that weightUdp=0.3035 exceeds 1% loss.

claims.text: The scheduler gives TCP the link share not used by UDP when UDP is not backlogged, so TCP is not capped by 1-weightUdp at high weightUdp.
The UDP-loss threshold for queuePkts=100 and TcpCubic lies between weightUdp=0.3030 and 0.3035: 0.3030 has udp_loss_frac=0.011155, while 0.3035 has udp_loss_frac=0.009736.
Allowing UDP loss up to the 1% limit raises TCP goodput because unserved UDP capacity is used by TCP; the best tested feasible point is weightUdp=0.3035 with tcp_goodput_bps=671509421.

Increasing queuePkts does not materially increase TCP goodput at the threshold; q50 and q200 at weightUdp=0.3030 match q100's UDP loss and TCP goodput, while q1000 at weightUdp=0.35 lowered TCP goodput.
Very small queues do not provide a feasible TCP gain: q4 at weightUdp=0.30 avoided UDP loss but did not raise TCP goodput, and q8 near weightUdp=0.3006 had many TCP drops and UDP loss above 1%.
At a UDP-safe scheduler setting, loss-based TCP variants are essentially tied, while BBR and Vegas underutilize the link; TcpCubic is therefore a safe choice.
Seed variation at weightUdp=0.3030 is negligible for the measured outputs, supporting seed=1 as a representative tested setting.

open_questions: The exact optimum between weightUdp=0.3035 and 0.3036 was not tested.
Whether queuePkts=8 at weightUdp=0.3035 is feasible and whether it could beat queuePkts=100 was not tested.
Whether duration=30 or seeds other than 1 at weightUdp=0.3035 would move udp_loss_frac across the 1% boundary was not tested.
The exact scheduler service discipline when one queue is not backlogged was inferred from behavior, not directly observed.
body.observations: X4 explored queuePkts=8 for weightUdp from 0.30005 to 0.30060. Every tested q8 run violated the UDP constraint: udp_loss_frac was 0.0131 for weightUdp=0.30005-0.30030 and 0.010379 for weightUdp=0.30040-0.30060 (E4). Therefore no tested q8 setting in that range is feasible. The best tested feasible setting remains w03035: weightUdp=0.3035, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, seed=1, duration=10, with tcp_goodput_bps=671509421 and udp_loss_frac=0.009736 (E3, C9). Nearby infeasible settings have higher TCP goodput: w03030 gives 671928762 with udp_loss_frac=0.011155 (E3), and q8_w030060 gives 671699398 with udp_loss_frac=0.010379 (E4). All earlier hypotheses have already received verdicts; no open decision-rule hypotheses remain.
